name: Omar Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the laying flock at Brookend, which is 32,000 free-range hens in two sheds, plus a bit of barley and grass that the owners farm around them. I'm up at five to walk the sheds before the lights come on, because you learn more in that half hour than in the rest of the day. Then it's the egg belts, the packing room with Rosa, the pop holes open at nine, and checking for foxes and red mite. At night I do the paperwork for the welfare audits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you're proudest of?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our mortality rate. Last flock we lost under four percent over the whole lay, which is very good for free range, and I did that by walking the sheds, not by staring at graphs. The part I'm not proud of is my bank balance. I rent a room above the farm office for cheap, I've got about two weeks' money saved, and I get paid like a junior even though the owners call me the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. I use a chatbot to tidy up my audit reports sometimes, and that's about as far as it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold, like most things that come with a big launch. It's handy for writing the boring letters, and that's it. Hens still need someone in the shed at five in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed and a bit relieved at once. I hoped it might take the paperwork off me so I could spend more time with the birds. The real fight in egg farming is the supermarket price, and AI was never going to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep using the chatbot for the audit write-ups, which saves me maybe two hours a week. I'd stay active in the poultry workers' group and keep pushing the owners for a pay rise tied to the egg price. If I could put twenty pounds a week aside, I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, the way you are when a new sprayer turns out the same as the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the supermarket price. Who do you hold responsible for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four big buyers who set it. They squeezed egg prices for years while feed doubled, and farms like ours took it because there's nobody else to sell to. If AI was a bust, that's still the story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two extra hours a week from the chatbot actually go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking the sheds, honestly. I'd find the hen with a bad foot an hour earlier. Or I'd sleep, which my mum keeps telling me to do.

S0.say: I'd say AI was oversold like most things with a big launch, handy for boring letters and nothing more. Hens still need someone in the shed at five in the morning.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed and a bit relieved, because I hoped it would take the paperwork off me. The real fight is the supermarket egg price, which AI was never going to fix.
S0.do: Keeps running the flock and uses the chatbot for audit reports, saving about two hours a week. Stays active in the poultry workers' group and pushes for pay tied to the egg price.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly let down, like a new sprayer that turns out the same as the old one.
S0.quote: Hens still need someone in the shed at five in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is quietly proud and very precise, quoting his mortality rate without being asked. He already uses AI a little and is mildly disappointed it doesn't do more. His anger is aimed at supermarket buyers, not technology. The time he'd save goes straight back to the birds, which says a lot about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I can actually picture. The egg graders and the camera systems are already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be good for hens and workers if it's done properly, and bad if it's just about cutting staff. I'd say it at the poultry group and online. I'd want the workers on the farm to have a say in which machines come in and what happens to the saved wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it could be good for me, as long as I move with it. Somebody has to run the camera systems and the robot that picks up floor eggs, and I'd rather it was me than a salesman. My worry is Rosa in the packing room, because a grading machine with AI could do her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of farms nearby had tried the shed cameras and the floor-egg robot, then ask to trial one here. I'd do a short course on the poultry software the supplier offers, probably in the winter when the flock is settled. And I'd push the owners to move Rosa to bird welfare checks instead of letting her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than I expected. It's change I could steer a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for other farms first, rather than trying it straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a bad robot in a laying shed causes panic and pile-ups, and hens die in pile-ups. I've seen it with a new lighting system that flickered. I'll be second, not first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you put it to Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight over our tea break, because she'd smell it if I didn't. Then I'd say I'm pushing for her to do the welfare walks with me. She knows those birds as well as I do.

S1.say: I'd say this can be good for hens and workers if done properly, and bad if it's only about cutting staff. Workers should get a say in which machines come in and where the savings go.
S1.think: I think it could be good for me if I move with it, since someone has to run the cameras and robots. My worry is Rosa in the packing room, whose job a grading machine could take.
S1.do: Waits until nearby farms have tried shed cameras and a floor-egg robot, then asks to trial one. Takes the supplier's poultry software course over winter and pushes the owners to move Rosa into welfare checks.
S1.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than he expected, because this is change he could steer.
S1.fieldNote: Omar's caution is about animal welfare, not fear: a flickering light once caused a pile-up, and that shapes his rule of going second. He sees a role for himself running the new kit. His concern for Rosa is concrete and practical. His progressive views come out as workers having a say, not as opposition to the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's barely more than one flock cycle. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is going too fast for anyone to manage it fairly. Online I'd say the companies building it should be taxed hard and that money should keep rural workers going. I'd also say someone has to check the robots are treating animals right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm out. A machine that walks a shed, spots a sick hen and runs the audits doesn't need a manager on low pay, it needs a contract with the supplier. And my room is above the farm office, so if I lose the job I lose my bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd stop the little things: the gym, the streaming, the car finance if I could hand it back. I'd sign up to every worker group pushing for a basic income and write to the agriculture minister. In the year after, I'd probably go back to my parents' flat in the city and look for whatever work there is, even if it's nothing to do with birds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the same feeling as when the bird flu letter comes and you know the whole flock might go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change for you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is less than a flock. I can't save on what I earn, I can't finish a course, I can't even see what the new jobs are before they're gone. With longer I'd move with it, like I said for the slower one. With two years I just get carried along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. Would you try to become the person who runs the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask, definitely. But if it can run itself, why would the owners pay me to watch it? Maybe for a year as a handover, and then I think they'd thank me and that would be that.

S2.say: I'd say this is moving too fast for anyone to manage fairly. The companies building it should be taxed hard to keep rural workers going, and someone must check robots treat animals right.
S2.think: I think I'm out, because a machine that walks the shed and runs the audits doesn't need a low-paid manager. My room is above the farm office, so losing the job means losing my bed.
S2.do: Cancels the gym and streaming at once and tries to hand back the car finance. Joins groups pushing for a basic income, writes to the agriculture minister, and expects to move back to his parents' flat in the city.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the day the bird flu letter arrives and the whole flock might go.
S2.quote: Two years is less than a flock.
S2.fieldNote: The speed undoes Omar's usual plan of going second, because there's no time to see what others do first. His tied room makes losing the job doubly hard, a detail he raised himself. He still offered to run the system but expects to be thanked and let go. His blame and his hopes both point at taxes on AI companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's three or four flocks. Still quick, but I could do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the government and the owners as much as us workers. I'd push for paid retraining and for rules that farm robots have to meet welfare standards. And I'd say it in the poultry group chat until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make myself the person who sets the robots up, at least for a while. I'd watch which systems win and get trained on that one. After that, I honestly don't know, but at least I wouldn't be caught with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save every month I possibly can, even if it's only thirty pounds, and stop putting things on the card. Once two or three farms near us had the new systems, I'd do the supplier's full training. I'd also start asking about welfare auditing jobs, because I already know that paperwork inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like the week before an audit: lots to do, but you know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop spending on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the car. I'd sell the car and borrow the farm pickup when I need it, which the owners have said is fine. That alone would be about a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about welfare auditing. Couldn't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could do the checklist, yes. But somebody has to be legally responsible when birds suffer, and I'd want that to be a person. I'd be campaigning for that rule as much as for my own job.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them, and that goes for government and owners too. I'd push for paid retraining and welfare standards for farm robots.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to become the person who sets up the robots, at least for a while. After that I honestly don't know, but I wouldn't be caught with nothing.
S3.do: Sells his car to save about a hundred and fifty a month and stops using his credit card. Does the supplier's full training once nearby farms adopt the systems and starts asking about welfare auditing work.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, like the week before an audit when there's a lot to do but he knows what.
S3.quote: Somebody has to be legally responsible when birds suffer, and I'd want that to be a person.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Omar's careful style works again: he can watch which system wins and then train on it. Selling the car was a concrete and fairly painful cut. His job hope and his political demand are the same thing, a human legally responsible for animal welfare. He is honest that the longer-term picture is blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven. That's time to have a whole career change, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. I'd want unions and colleges setting up real routes out of farm work now, and I'd want it paid for by the companies that will profit. Publicly I'd sound fairly calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd use the first few years to get really good at the new poultry systems, and the later ones to move into something with a human sign-off, like auditing or farm vet work. I've thought about vet nursing before. It's a lot of studying, but in ten years I could do it part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start the poultry systems training and set up a small standing order to savings, even fifty pounds. By year two or three I'd apply for a part-time veterinary nursing course and ask the owners to let me work four days. I wouldn't rush; I'd see which way the first robots go on other farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. There's room to breathe and room to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in eggs at all, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a few years. I like the birds, but I don't love the egg business, it's always been a squeeze. If robots run the sheds, I'd rather be the person checking they're doing it kindly than the person keeping the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about vet nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say about time. She always wanted me to do something with a certificate on the wall. She'd also say I should eat more and sleep more, which is fair.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and nobody should be left behind. Unions and colleges should open real routes out of farm work now, paid for by the companies that profit.
S4.think: I think I'd master the new poultry systems first and then move into a job with a human sign-off, like auditing or vet nursing. Ten years is enough to study part-time.
S4.do: Starts poultry systems training and a fifty-pound monthly savings order in year one. Applies for part-time veterinary nursing study in year two or three and asks to work four days, while watching how robots go on other farms.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, with room to breathe and choose.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the person checking they're doing it kindly than the person keeping the lights on.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years opens a real plan, vet nursing, that Omar had clearly thought about before. He separates his love of the birds from the egg business, which he finds a constant squeeze. His pace is still careful: train, watch, then move. His mother's voice keeps showing up, and she clearly matters to his choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the job and the room in one go, with two weeks of money. What would help is a basic income or a wage while you retrain, paid for by the AI companies, and a law that a person signs off on animal welfare, so there's still a job for people who care about the birds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. Everyone talks about jobs, and I care about jobs, but a robot that gets it wrong in a laying shed can kill thousands of birds in an hour. I'd want someone to ask who's responsible before they switch anything on.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person checking they're doing it kindly than the person keeping the lights on.
portrait: Omar Tanaka is 27 and manages 32,000 free-range hens, with an excellent welfare record and a junior's pay packet. He lives in a cheap room above the farm office and has about two weeks of savings. He uses AI now and then for paperwork and follows a simple rule with new kit: go second, after someone else has proved it. In the slower scenarios he sees himself running the new systems and moving towards welfare auditing or vet nursing; in the two-year picture he expects to lose his job and his room together and go back to his parents in the city. His worries keep returning to the birds and to a co-worker, Rosa.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would lose his job and the room he lives in at once, with only two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or a paid wage while retraining, funded by AI companies, and a law that a person must sign off on animal welfare.
